HOLIDAY ABROAD® IN LONDON
REG OWEN and His Orchestra
Everyone has one place he prefers above all others, I suppose, and mine is London.
I love the town. I love the way the buildings look-severe and austere and dignified,
but gay with flowered window-boxes. I love to stand around in a pub like The White
Bear and watch the dim light reflected in the burnished woodwork. I love the march-
ing bands in the streets, blaring forth jazz, and I love the terrible jokes of the grinning
comedians in the music halls. I love to sit in a theater with a drink by my elbow (the
London theater makes the New York theater all but unbearable). I love to go to the
Poets Corner at Westminster Abbey and stand for minutes-even hours-marveling
at the vast talents that lie buried there, secure in the knowledge that their work will
live forever. I love the demonstrations and mass meetings in Trafalgar Square, the
men who hawk newspapers and the newspapers themselves, and the deferential clerks
in the stores. I love to go into Grafton Street and spend a long time with Mr. Dingle
of F. Tautz deciding what material he will use for my next suit, and then I love to
go around to the Westbury Hotel and have a glass of scotch with Tony, the manager.
I love to wander up and down Fleet Street, where it is impossible for an American
to tell the journalists from the barristers, and then I love to go and meet Nico Davies,
a publisher friend of mine, in his tradition-laden club, The Garrick. I love to ride on
the top deck of the double-decker buses, and I love to dodge the bicycles and the
queer little motorbikes. I love the richly-appointed lobby of The Savoy Hotel, where
one confronts the most famous people in the world. I love the BBC and its talks on
birds and weeds and thrips. I love the skife bands and the jam sessions in the stone-
walled cellar of The Cottage in Litchfield Street. I love the bookshops and the
newsstands. I love the bawdy talk at the weekly meetings of The Thursday Club,
that high-spirited group of stags, and I love the forty-odd varieties of Dover sole one
gets in the Wheeler restaurants. I love the air of reserve and hauteur in Belgrave
Square, and I love the intimacy of the mews and keeps just off it. I love the well-
groomed English women and the red-checked children. There is practically nothing
about London I do not love-and finally, I love Reg Owen for putting a musical
picture of the town I love on this record.
RICHARD GEHMAN
